claims.proposition_evaluated: Documented, occupied low-density housing (one or two dwellings on an identified lot, branch (b) for Claim A) existed inside Edmonton's boundary in force at the time in calendar year 1926, at the 2026-09-01 endpoint, and at least once in each city-wide bylaw era between, over the exact window 1926-09-01 to 2026-09-01.
claims.interpretation_notes: Applied the brief's fixed test: one qualifying occupied lot in 1926 (calendar-year reading primary), an endpoint observation, and one observation per era. Eras used, from the City's History of Zoning and Historical Land Use Bylaws guide: no city-wide zoning instrument 1926-09-01 to 1933-10-10; Zoning Bylaw 26, 1933-10-10 to 1950-10-17; Interim Development Bylaw 1339, 1950-10-17 to 1959-09-01; Interim Development Bylaw No. 2, 1959-09-01 to October 1961 (the History calls it Bylaw 1998, the resource guide lists it as bylaw no. 1988; discrepancy unresolved); Zoning Bylaw 2135, October 1961 to 1980-07-03; Land Use Bylaw 5996, 1980-07-03 to 2001-06-14; Zoning Bylaw 12800, 2001-06-14 to 2024-01-01; Zoning Bylaw 20001, 2024-01-01 onward (Council passed 2023-10-23; amendments through Bylaw 21538, adopted 2026-07-06, per the official register). Observations obtained: 1926 (Henderson's 1926 street directory, Ada Boulevard, Highlands, householder Bidwell A Holgate at the Holgate Residence lot, 6210 Ada Boulevard, a house on a single lot built 1912; Highlands inside Edmonton since the 1911-12-20 annexation per the City's annexation dataset), 1935 and 1946 (Henderson's, householders at 5650 and 5222 Ada Boulevard, Highlands), 1956 (Henderson's, Ada Blvd Highlands Subdivision, householders at 5014, 5022 and onward), 1964 (Henderson's, householder at 4442 Ada Blvd, in the Beverly area annexed 1961-12-31), 2021 (federal census, 196,535 occupied single-detached houses), and January 2026 (City assessment: 440,051 properties, median single-family detached home $492,500 CAD; the 2025 report counts 1,077 single-family detached properties in Highlands and 1,152 in Glenora as of 2024-12-31). No observation was obtained for the Land Use Bylaw 5996 era (1980-07-03 to 2001-06-14), so the fixed per-era test is not fully met by my evidence; the longest interval between observations is 1964 to 2021 (57 years). The 1996 and 2001 census dwelling-type tables exist but I could not retrieve the Edmonton rows. Indirect evidence for that era: the City's 2005 municipal-census profile of Parkallen describes the neighbourhood as dominated by single-detached bungalows built by 1960, which must have stood through 1980-2001. Exact-date result (1926-09-01): the 1926 directory is an annual compilation with no day-specific date, so the exact-day observation is not separately established; the calendar-year test is met. Legal permission reported separately: no zoning instrument existed in 1926; Bylaw 26 (1933) created a One-family Dwelling District per the City's History (bylaw text not obtained; Issuu copy inaccessible to me); RF1 districts in Bylaws 5996 and 12800 were labelled Single Detached; the RS zone in force on 2026-09-01 permits up to 8 dwellings on interior sites and is not low density under the brief's rule, so at the endpoint built low-density housing exists without a low-density-labelled city-wide zone.

claims.suggested_one_line: Occupied single-detached houses are documented in Edmonton's Highlands in 1926 and in nearly every zoning era since, so low-density housing has existed for about a century, though my record has a 1980-2001 gap.
claims.suggested_short_answer: Henderson's 1926 directory lists householders on Ada Boulevard in the Highlands, annexed in 1911, and the same street shows occupied houses in 1935, 1946, 1956 and 1964. The 2021 census counts 196,535 single-detached houses and the City's 2026 assessment roll values a median single-family home at $492,500. Zoning is a separate question: no zoning bylaw existed in 1926, the first (Bylaw 26) came in 1933, and the zone in force today allows up to eight dwellings on a small-scale residential lot.
suggested_tldr: Occupied single-lot houses in the Highlands appear in the 1926 city directory; Highlands was inside Edmonton from 1911.
Later directories (1935, 1946, 1956, 1964), the 2021 census and the 2026 assessment roll show the housing type continuing.
No observation was retrieved for 1980-2001; the longest gap between observations is 57 years.
Zoning permission is a different story: none in 1926, single-family districts from 1933 to 2023, and an 8-dwelling small-scale zone since 2024.

claims.proposition_evaluated: Under the primary readings fixed in the brief: at least 10 present-day City of Edmonton neighbourhood polygons were, at some point between 1926-09-01 and 2026-09-01 and while inside Edmonton's boundary then in force, named or mapped by a published neighbourhood-specific plan, subdivision document, covenant, developer plan or official historical report stating that low-density housing (branch (a) era terminology or branch (b) no more than two principal dwellings per lot) was a principal or predominant planned residential form.
claims.interpretation_notes: Primary count result: 10 neighbourhoods counted, meeting the cutoff of 10 exactly; the alternative cutoff of 5 is met. Counted (plan, adoption date, operative statement, boundary check from the City annexation dataset): Lymburn (NSP Bylaw 6033, 1980-07-09; Single Detached 944 units, 90.5 percent of units; West Jasper Place annexed 1972-01-01); Ozerna (NSP Bylaw 6385, 1981-03-24; Low Density Residential 66.25 ha, 1,193 units, 81.3 percent; Lake District annexed 1971-01-01); Cumberland (NSP Bylaw 7563, 1984-06-19; 'Low density is proposed at 83%', 'The emphasis of housing for this Neighbourhood is on Low Density Residential'; annexed 1982-01-01); Oxford (NSP Bylaw 7963, 1985-09-10; Low Density Residential 52.9 ha, 927 units, 74.1 percent; annexed 1982); Silver Berry (NSP Bylaw 10818, 1994-12-14; Low Density Residential 75.67 ha, 1,286 units, 70.97 percent; annexed 1982); Carlton (NSP Bylaw 12001, 1999-04-26; 'Low density residential is 72% ... of the total dwelling units'; annexed 1982); Tamarack (NSP Bylaw 14112, 2006-02-22; Low Density Residential Single/Semi-detached 89.04 ha, 2,226 units, LDR/MDR ratio 72/28; annexed 1982); Stewart Greens (NSP Bylaw 14674, 2007-08-21; 'Low-density residential development will occupy approximately 27 ha of land mostly in the form of single-detached housing', LDR to MDR ratio about 52 to 48; annexed 1982; weakest entry because the shares are near parity); Laurel (NSP Bylaw 14622, July 2007; states the plan 'maintains a housing mix unit ratio within the recommended' guideline of 65 to 85 percent low density residential; annexed 1982); Kendal (NSP Bylaw 21113, 2025-04-28; Low Density Residential 127.99 ha, 3,839 units, 76.0 percent of net residential area; within the Windermere ASP area annexed 1982). All ten meet branch (a) through the plans' own 'Low Density Residential' or 'Single Detached' designations; branch (b) is also met for Lymburn (RF1/RPL/RSL single detached). Era-by-era counts (firm): no-zoning era 1926-1933: 0; Bylaw 26 era: 0; Interim Development era: 0; Bylaw 2135 era: 0 firm (Riverbend ASP, Bylaw 5710, 1979-09-12, names six neighbourhoods, Bulyea Heights, Rhatigan Ridge, Henderson Estates, Falconer Heights, Ogilvie Ridge, Carter Crest, 'designated for low-medium density development' and 'low density development for Riverbend' at 40-55 persons per gross hectare; treated as borderline, not counted; land annexed 1959-12-30); Land Use Bylaw 5996 era: 6; Zoning Bylaw 12800 era: 3; Zoning Bylaw 20001 era: 1. Borderline or unextracted, not counted: Riverbend's six; Walker, Ellerslie, Secord, Windermere, The Hamptons, Summerside, Eaux Claires and Klarvatten NSPs all designate Low Density Residential areas but I could not extract their land-use tables, so no share was obtained; Mill Woods Development Concept (Council resolution, March 1971; Mill Woods annexed 1971-01-01) plans 38.2 percent low density dwellings and 60 percent multiple accommodation overall and names sectors rather than present-day neighbourhoods, so it adds nothing to the count and is partial contrary evidence. Pre-window context only: Glenora's 1911 Carruthers caveat ('detached or semi-detached', one dwelling per lot; Groat Estate inside Edmonton from the 1904 incorporation or 1908 annexation) and the Highlands 1910 Magrath-Holgate subdivision (minimum house value; land annexed 1911-12-20, so planning predates annexation) were planned before 1926-09-01 and enter no calculation. Westmount: same covenant wording reported but registration date and area not established from a published source; not counted. End-of-window reading (2026-09-01): the counted NSPs remain in effect with their Low Density Residential designations (office consolidations dated 2021-2025), but the city-wide zoning instrument, Zoning Bylaw 20001, no longer carries a low-density-labelled standard zone; instrument (RS, up to 8 dwellings) and statutory-plan designation diverge, so the end-of-window count on plans alone is 10 and on zoning alone is 0. Share reading: no published complete roster with low-density flags was found for any era; no share calculated. Contemporaneous-unit reading: NSP boundaries coincide with present-day polygons in these cases, so the result is the same 10; no historical subdivision boundaries were obtained for pre-1980 eras. Residential-land share and dwellings-per-hectare: not calculated; the plans state target densities (e.g. 25 or 30 units per net residential hectare for LDR) as sensitivities only. City-wide context not counted: the City's History of Zoning says Bylaw 26 (1933-10-10) 'largely favoured low-density development of single-family homes, with a majority of the lots in the city zoned One-Family Unit District' (secondary description; bylaw text not obtained), and RF1 in Bylaws 5996 (1998 consolidation read) and 12800 (2001 text read) was labelled Single Detached with 360 m2 minimum site area and 'a maximum of one Dwelling per lot' except where semi-detached, duplex or secondary suites were allowed (later, by Charter Bylaw 18638 of 2018-12-10, those became permitted uses in RF1, so a lot could hold two principal dwellings plus suites; borderline under branch (b), still branch (a) by label). A 1991 Council guideline of 65 to 85 percent low-density units for new suburban neighbourhoods is quoted in the Walker and Laurel NSPs.

challenging_evidence.finding: The Mill Woods Development Concept (approved by Council resolution March 1971, after the 1971-01-01 annexation) planned 'a potential total dwelling stock of some 33,000 units, generally comprised of 60% in the form of multiple accommodation'; its housing component table gives Low Density Dwellings 11,200 (38.2 percent), Horizontal Multiple 7,300 (25.1 percent), Vertical Multiple 8,000 (27.1 percent) plus public housing, and 'within the low density neighbourhoods, some 60-70% of the net residential land area has been allocated to single family use'.

challenging_evidence.establishes: Edmonton's largest 1970s plan was not planned around low-density housing overall; it names sectors, not present-day neighbourhoods, so it neither adds to nor subtracts from the count, but it shows that 'many' is not 'all' or 'most'.
challenging_evidence.quote: generally comprised of 60% in the form of multiple accommodation

challenging_evidence.finding: Zoning Bylaw 20001, in force at the end of the window, has no low-density-labelled standard zone; the RS Small Scale Residential Zone permits up to 8 dwellings on interior sites and its purpose covers 'detached, attached, and multi-unit Residential housing'. Zoning Bylaw 12800's RF1 zone had already been amended (Charter Bylaw 18638, 2018-12-10) to permit Semi-detached, Duplex, Secondary Suites and Garden Suites outright, its purpose reading 'to provide for Single Detached Housing while allowing other forms of small scale housing'.

limitations: The primary count is exactly 10, at the cutoff. Two entries (Stewart Greens, Laurel) rest on qualitative or guideline statements rather than a plan-specific share; removing both would give 8, below the cutoff, which is why confidence is Moderate rather than High.

Eight further NSPs I read (Walker, Ellerslie, Secord, Windermere, The Hamptons, Summerside, Eaux Claires, Klarvatten) designate Low Density Residential areas but their land-use tables did not extract legibly, so no share was obtained and none was counted; the true count is very likely higher than 10.

Era-by-era firm counts: 1926-1933: 0; Bylaw 26 era: 0; Interim era: 0; Bylaw 2135 era: 0 (Riverbend's six borderline); Bylaw 5996 era: 6; Bylaw 12800 era: 3; Bylaw 20001 era: 1. Alternative cutoff of 5: met. End-of-window reading: 10 on statutory plans still in effect, 0 on the zoning instrument alone.

No count was made for 1926-1980 neighbourhoods such as Parkallen, Crestwood or Sherbrooke: the Edmonton Historical Board pages give development dates and Noel Dant's 1950s planning of west Westmount but no published plan text stating the intended housing form, and the 1933, 1950 and 1961 bylaw texts and maps were not obtained.
Pre-window planning (Glenora 1911 covenant, Highlands 1910 subdivision, Westmount covenant) is context only and enters no count; Highlands' subdivision also predates its 1911-12-20 annexation.

Share reading, covered-area share, residential-land share and contemporaneous-unit results: not calculated; no published roster or geometry was found for any era. The City neighbourhood polygon layer (Neighbourhoods, FeatureServer layer 35) has 407 features and was used only to confirm that each counted plan name is a present-day neighbourhood.

Classification of Bylaw 26 (1933) and Bylaw 2135 (1961) residential districts rests on the City's History of Zoning, a secondary description; count of borderline instruments: 3 (Bylaw 26 'B' district and Bylaw 2135 R-1, text not obtained; late Bylaw 12800 RF1 after 2018, two principal dwellings plus suites). None was used in the count.
All plan quotations are from City office consolidations, which state that the original bylaws govern; adoption dates are as recorded in each consolidation's amendment list.

If the article reports NSP shares, state each plan's own denominator (units, net residential area or gross area) as quoted; they differ between plans.
what_would_change_my_verdict: Showing that two or more of the ten counted plans do not treat low-density housing as a principal form (for example, that Laurel's actual unit mix fell below 50 percent low density), which would drop the count below 10.
Evidence that any counted neighbourhood lay outside Edmonton's boundary at its plan's adoption date (the City dataset places all ten inside).
Extracted tables for the eight unread NSPs would likely raise the count well above 10 and lift confidence to High.
claims.suggested_one_line: At least ten Edmonton neighbourhoods, from Lymburn in 1980 to Kendal in 2025, have City-adopted plans that make low-density housing the main planned form, so 'many neighbourhoods were planned around it' holds, though the count sits right at the cutoff and Edmonton's biggest 1970s plan, Mill Woods, was 60 percent multi-family.
claims.suggested_short_answer: Ten present-day neighbourhoods inside Edmonton's boundary at the time have published neighbourhood structure plans stating that low-density or single-detached housing was the predominant planned form: Lymburn (1980, 90.5 percent of units single detached), Ozerna (1981), Cumberland (1984), Oxford (1985), Silver Berry (1994), Carlton (1999), Tamarack (2006), Stewart Greens (2007), Laurel (2007) and Kendal (2025). That meets the brief's cutoff of ten exactly, with eight more plans designating low-density areas whose tables I could not read. Pre-1926 planning such as Glenora's 1911 one-house-per-lot covenant is context only. The Mill Woods concept of 1971 planned 60 percent multiple housing, and the zoning bylaw in force since 2024 has no single-detached zone, so the claim is true of many neighbourhoods, not of the city as a whole.
suggested_tldr: Ten neighbourhood plans adopted between 1980 and 2025 state low-density housing as the predominant planned form; cutoff of ten met exactly.
Era counts: none confirmed for 1926-1980 (plans not obtained or ambiguous), six for 1980-2001, three for 2001-2024, one since 2024.
Glenora's 1911 covenant and Highlands' 1910 subdivision predate the window and are context only.
Counter-evidence: Mill Woods (1971) planned 60 percent multi-family; the current RS zone allows up to eight dwellings per lot.
